cells.tense: Clear sight is arriving now and the weak structures are going down quietly, on their own schedule.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've already outgrown and write it on a slip. Keep the slip where you work, and let the paper hold it instead of your head.
cells.core:
When a structure is false, it comes down fast once you see it clearly. You're seeing. Something you built on a wrong guess is loosening, and it isn't falling on you — it's falling away, which is the easy kind. You get to watch it happen without bracing.

The room this leaves isn't empty, it's usable. What holds after a clearing gets built by repetition, not by flashes, so keep the quiet practice going at the same pace. Same time, same small piece, refined a little each round. That's what makes the next thing stand instead of wobble. Nothing here needs force from you — the sight is already doing its work.
cells.sheetLine: The false part is already coming down. You're just watching it.

cells.tense: A collapse somewhere ahead is being lived through now, so everything in reach gets knocked down before it can be tested.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you planned to tear up this week and use it once more instead. See whether it actually fails — that's your data.
cells.core:
You're ahead of the event. Some structure is going to fall, so you're pre-demolishing everything within reach — the job, the arrangement, the version of yourself that's been working — and calling the wreckage freedom. It isn't yet. It's just early.

Real clearings follow seeing. Yours is running in front of it. Try this instead: take one thing you've already written off and use it again, deliberately, for a day. Ask someone who's been at this longer how they do it, and let their way carry you a week. What you didn't invent yourself can hold while the one true thing falls.
cells.sheetLine: You're knocking things down before you've seen they can't hold.

cells.tense: Something finished earlier is still being held up, and the effort of holding it is quietly running the days.
cells.ask: Put one thing you've been propping up onto paper — what it was for, what still uses it. Let the day finish with that on paper.
cells.core:
You're holding up something that stopped holding. Not loud — nobody sees the strain, which is the problem. Its use ran out and you kept the beams in place, so now your hands are full and the doorway behind you is still open, unnoticed.

What's needed isn't more will. It's shape: a clear, modest arrangement that tells you what still works and what doesn't. Put one thing you've been propping up onto paper — what it was for, what actually still uses it. The answer tends to be smaller than the prop. Set it down there, beside you, and let the rest of the day go to something that stands by itself.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding up a door that stopped being a door.

cells.tense: The pen is already moving on what falls next, while the hand holding it says nothing is being decided.
cells.ask: Say one sentence naming which arrangement you've quietly stopped keeping up, then take one small step on it today.
cells.core:
Something in your life is coming down, and you're the one who decided that — in a shrug, a silence, a plan you keep not saying. You'd describe the situation as just what's happening. But people who leave a thing usually know before they leave. You know first.

Ask what you actually want, not what the arrangement requires, and you get a direction, not a mood. That direction is already doing the demolition, quietly, without your name on it. Put your name on it. One honest sentence about which thing you've stopped keeping up, said to another person or said plainly to yourself, and the falling stops being something done to you.
cells.sheetLine: The clearing already started. You're the one who started it.
